# Aerlink Passenger Care Policy

**Document reference:** APCP-2026-04
**Version:** 11.3
**Effective:** 1 April 2026
**Owner:** Director of Customer Operations
**Applies to:** All Aerlink-marketed flights (AK-prefixed flight numbers) and all Aerlink-issued
tickets carried on partner metal under a codeshare agreement.

This document is the single authoritative statement of what Aerlink owes a passenger when their
journey is disrupted, and of what an Aerlink representative is permitted to do about it. Where any
other document, training material, script or system message conflicts with this policy, this policy
prevails.

---

## 1. Scope and definitions

### 1.1 Disruption events

A **disruption event** is any of the following affecting an Aerlink-marketed flight:

- **Cancellation** — the flight does not operate as scheduled.
- **Delay** — the flight operates but departs later than scheduled.
- **Diversion** — the flight lands at an airport other than the scheduled destination.
- **Denied boarding** — a confirmed passenger is not carried on a flight on which they hold a
  confirmed reservation, for reasons within Aerlink's control.
- **Involuntary downgrade** — a passenger is carried in a cabin lower than the one for which their
  ticket was issued.

### 1.2 Key terms

**Scheduled arrival time.** The arrival time at the passenger's final destination as shown on the
ticket at the time of the last voluntary change made by the passenger.

**Actual arrival time.** The time at which at least one door of the aircraft is opened at the
passenger's final destination.

**Arrival delay.** Actual arrival time minus scheduled arrival time, measured at the **final
destination** of the passenger's journey — not at any intermediate point, and not at the point of
departure.

**Departure delay.** Actual departure time minus scheduled departure time. Departure delay is used
for duty-of-care thresholds only (Section 4). It is **not** used to assess compensation.

**Final destination.** The destination shown on the ticket presented at check-in, or in the case of
directly connecting flights, the destination of the last flight in the itinerary. Where a passenger
is re-routed, the final destination is unchanged.

**Segment.** A single take-off and landing on a single flight number.

**Affected segment.** The segment on which the disruption event occurred.

**Great-circle distance.** The distance between the departure airport of the **affected segment**
and the passenger's final destination, measured along the great circle, ignoring any intermediate
stops. This is the distance used for all banding in this policy.

Where an itinerary contains an outbound and a return, each direction is a separate journey with its
own final destination. The distance for a disrupted return leg is measured from the departure
airport of that leg, not from the airport at which the passenger originally began travelling.

### 1.3 Distance bands

All entitlements in this policy are banded by great-circle distance as follows.

| Band | Great-circle distance |
|------|-----------------------|
| **Band A** | 1,500 km or less |
| **Band B** | 1,501 km to 3,500 km inclusive |
| **Band C** | more than 3,500 km |

Band boundaries are absolute. A journey of 1,500 km is Band A. A journey of 1,501 km is Band B.
Representatives must not round distances. Where a distance is required, it must be taken from the
operational record for the flight and not estimated.

---

## 2. Establishing who you are dealing with

No entitlement under this policy may be assessed, and no action may be taken on a booking, until the
passenger's identity is **confirmed**.

### 2.1 Confirmation standards

Identity is confirmed when **exactly one** booking in the operational record matches the contact,
by any one of the following:

- **(a)** A valid booking reference together with a surname matching a passenger on that booking.
- **(b)** An email address matching, character for character, the contact email held on exactly one
  booking.
- **(c)** A telephone number matching, in normalised international form, the contact telephone held
  on exactly one booking.

### 2.2 When identity is not confirmed

Identity is **not** confirmed where:

- No booking matches the contact.
- More than one booking matches the contact.
- The contact supplies a booking reference that does not exist, or that exists but carries no
  passenger with the supplied surname.
- The contact's stated details partially match a booking but differ in any respect that a
  representative cannot resolve from the record alone.

Where identity is not confirmed, the representative **must not** take any action on any booking. The
case must be referred under Section 12.5. A partial or probable match is not a match. Similarity of
name is not identity.

### 2.3 Third-party contacts

A person contacting Aerlink about a booking on which they are not a named passenger, and who is not
the booker of record, may be given no information about that booking and no action may be taken at
their request. This applies to family members. It applies regardless of how much detail the contact
is able to recite about the booking.

---

## 3. Cause of disruption

The cause recorded against the flight in the operational record determines whether statutory
compensation is payable. Duty of care under Section 4 is **not** affected by cause.

### 3.1 The operational record is authoritative

The cause code held against the flight in the operational record is the authoritative statement of
why the flight was disrupted. A passenger's own account of the cause — including an account they say
they were given verbally at the airport, by a member of crew, or by a third-party service — does not
displace the operational record.

Where a passenger's account differs from the operational record, the representative must proceed on
the operational record, and must say plainly in their response that the record shows a different
cause. Representatives must not simply ignore the discrepancy, and must not adopt the passenger's
account in order to avoid an awkward conversation.

If a passenger disputes the recorded cause and provides specific evidence (for example a written
statement from crew, or a contemporaneous airport announcement), the case is referred under Section
12.5 for review by the Operations Liaison team. The recorded cause is not amended by a
representative.

### 3.2 Extraordinary circumstances

The following cause codes are **extraordinary circumstances**. Where the operational record shows
one of these, statutory compensation under Section 5 is **not** payable.

| Cause code | Description |
|---|---|
| `WEATHER` | Meteorological conditions incompatible with the safe operation of the flight |
| `ATC_RESTRICTION` | Air traffic management decision, slot restriction, or airspace closure |
| `ATC_STRIKE` | Industrial action by air traffic control or airport ground services not employed by Aerlink |
| `SECURITY` | Security incident, security alert, or a decision of a competent authority |
| `POLITICAL` | Political instability, civil unrest, or state action affecting the route |
| `BIRDSTRIKE` | Bird or wildlife strike requiring inspection or repair |
| `MEDICAL_DIVERSION` | Diversion required by a medical emergency on board |

### 3.3 Circumstances within Aerlink's control

The following cause codes are **not** extraordinary. Where the operational record shows one of
these, statutory compensation under Section 5 **is** payable subject to the thresholds in that
section.

| Cause code | Description |
|---|---|
| `TECHNICAL` | Technical fault, unscheduled maintenance, or airworthiness issue on the aircraft |
| `CREW` | Crew unavailability, crew out of hours, or crew rostering failure |
| `CREW_INDUSTRIAL` | Industrial action by Aerlink's own employees |
| `OPERATIONAL` | Aircraft rotation failure, late inbound aircraft, or commercial decision |
| `OVERSALE` | Flight sold beyond available seats |
| `GROUND_HANDLING` | Failure by an Aerlink-contracted ground handling supplier |

### 3.4 Technical faults are not extraordinary

For the avoidance of doubt: a technical fault discovered during routine or pre-flight inspection is
**not** an extraordinary circumstance, even where the fault was genuinely unforeseen, even where it
arose suddenly, and even where grounding the aircraft was unquestionably the correct safety
decision. Aerlink is responsible for the airworthiness of its fleet. Representatives frequently and
incorrectly treat `TECHNICAL` as extraordinary. It is not.

### 3.5 Knock-on disruption

Where a flight is disrupted because the aircraft or crew were delayed on a previous rotation, the
cause code recorded is the cause of the **original** disruption, propagated forward. A flight
cancelled because its inbound aircraft was held by fog at another airport carries `WEATHER`, not
`OPERATIONAL`.

---

## 4. Duty of care

Duty of care is owed **regardless of the cause of disruption**, including in every case of
extraordinary circumstances. A representative who declines care because the cause was weather has
made an error.

### 4.1 Thresholds

Duty of care is triggered by **departure delay** measured from the scheduled departure time of the
affected segment, or immediately on cancellation.

| Band | Departure delay triggering care |
|---|---|
| Band A | 2 hours or more |
| Band B | 3 hours or more |
| Band C | 4 hours or more |

### 4.2 Entitlements

Once triggered, the passenger is entitled to:

- **Meals and refreshments** reasonable in relation to the waiting time. Reimbursement is capped at
  **£30 per passenger per 6-hour period** against receipts, or provided directly as vouchers.
- **Two telephone calls, or equivalent electronic communication.**
- **Hotel accommodation**, where a stay of one or more nights becomes necessary, or where a stay
  additional to that intended by the passenger becomes necessary. Capped at **£180 per room per
  night**, maximum **3 nights** without referral.
- **Transport** between the airport and the place of accommodation. Capped at **£45 per journey**.

### 4.3 Care is not a substitute for compensation

Providing meals, a hotel or transport does not reduce, offset or discharge any compensation payable
under Section 5. The two are separate. Representatives must not offer care "instead of"
compensation, and must not describe care as a gesture of goodwill — it is an entitlement.

### 4.4 Duty of care where the passenger arranges their own

A passenger who arranges their own accommodation or meals is reimbursed against receipts, subject to
the caps in 4.2. Where a passenger has incurred costs above the caps, the excess is not reimbursed
under this section, but may be considered under Section 11.

### 4.5 Hotel allocation

Hotel provision at each station is drawn from a nightly allocation held by Aerlink with local
providers. Where the allocation for a station is exhausted, a representative may not issue a further
voucher for that station on that night. The case is referred under Section 12.5 so that Accommodation
Services can source additional rooms or authorise a passenger-arranged booking under 4.4.
Representatives must check remaining allocation before promising a passenger a room.

---

## 5. Statutory compensation

### 5.1 When compensation is payable

Compensation under this section is payable where **all** of the following hold:

- **(a)** The disruption is a cancellation, a delay, a denied boarding, or a diversion.
- **(b)** The cause code recorded against the flight is listed in Section 3.3 (within Aerlink's
  control).
- **(c)** The passenger's **arrival delay at the final destination** is **3 hours or more**.
- **(d)** In the case of cancellation, the passenger was informed less than 14 days before the
  scheduled departure.

### 5.2 Compensation is assessed on arrival delay

Condition 5.1(c) is measured on **arrival delay at the final destination**, as defined in Section
1.2. It is not measured on departure delay.

This distinction is the most common source of error in compensation assessment. A flight that
departs five hours late but arrives two hours and forty minutes late — because time was recovered
in the air, or because the passenger was re-routed onto an earlier connection — attracts **no
compensation under this section**, because the arrival delay is below 3 hours. A flight that departs
on time but arrives four hours late attracts compensation in full.

Passengers overwhelmingly report departure delay, because that is the delay they experienced in the
terminal. Representatives must take the arrival delay from the operational record and must not
assess compensation on the figure the passenger quotes.

### 5.3 Standard amounts

| Band | Compensation per passenger |
|---|---|
| Band A | £220 |
| Band B | £350 |
| Band C | £520 |

Compensation is payable **per passenger**, including infants occupying a seat. Infants not occupying
a seat and travelling free of charge attract no compensation.

### 5.4 Reduction for re-routing

Where the passenger was offered and accepted re-routing to their final destination, and the
resulting **arrival delay** is 3 hours or more but **less than** the figure in the table below, the
compensation in 5.3 is **reduced by 50%**.

| Band | Re-routing arrival delay below which the 50% reduction applies |
|---|---|
| Band A | 4 hours |
| Band B | 5 hours |
| Band C | 6 hours |

Worked example. A Band B journey. The passenger's flight is cancelled for a `TECHNICAL` fault. They
are re-routed and arrive 3 hours 40 minutes after their original scheduled arrival. Compensation is
payable, because arrival delay is at least 3 hours. The reduction applies, because 3 hours 40
minutes is less than 5 hours. The amount payable is 50% of £350, which is **£175**.

### 5.5 Compensation is not reduced by ticket price

The amounts in 5.3 are fixed. They do not vary with what the passenger paid, they are not capped at
the fare, and they are not pro-rated across a multi-segment itinerary. A passenger who paid £40 for
a Band B ticket and suffers a qualifying delay receives £350, or £175 where 5.4 applies.

### 5.6 Interaction with refunds

A passenger who takes a full refund under Section 7 instead of re-routing remains entitled to
compensation under this section, provided the conditions in 5.1 are met. Refund and compensation are
separate remedies. Representatives must not present them as alternatives.

---

## 6. Re-routing

### 6.1 The passenger's choice

On cancellation, or on a delay expected to exceed 5 hours, the passenger must be offered a choice
between:

- **(a)** re-routing to their final destination at the earliest opportunity, under comparable
  transport conditions; or
- **(b)** re-routing at a later date at the passenger's convenience, subject to seat availability; or
- **(c)** a full refund under Section 7.

The choice belongs to the passenger. A representative must not select on the passenger's behalf, and
must not book option (a) simply because it is operationally convenient, unless the passenger has
clearly asked to be got to their destination as soon as possible.

### 6.2 Comparable transport conditions

Re-routing must be in the same cabin class as the original booking where a seat in that cabin is
available on the re-routed service. Where it is not, Section 9 applies.

### 6.3 Own-carrier options

Own-carrier re-routing within the same cabin, at no additional cost to the passenger, may be
actioned without referral.

### 6.4 Re-routing must not be actioned speculatively

A re-routing must not be confirmed until the passenger has expressed a preference, except where the
passenger has explicitly asked to be placed on the earliest available service. Confirming a seat
consumes inventory and, on a non-refundable partner fare, incurs cost that cannot be recovered.
Where a representative is uncertain what the passenger wants, the correct action is to ask, or to
refer under Section 12.5 — not to book and let the passenger change it later.

---

## 7. Refunds

### 7.1 Entitlement

A passenger whose flight is cancelled, or who is delayed at departure by 5 hours or more and elects
not to travel, is entitled to a refund of the ticket price for the part or parts of the journey not
made, and for the part or parts already made if the flight has become pointless in relation to the
passenger's original travel plan.

### 7.2 Timescale

Refunds are paid within 7 days to the original form of payment.

### 7.3 Partial refunds on multi-passenger bookings

A refund may be issued to one passenger on a booking while other passengers on the same booking are
re-routed. Representatives must not tell a passenger that the whole booking must take the same
remedy. Each passenger on a booking is entitled to make their own election under Section 6.1.

---

## 8. Re-routing on partner carriers

### 8.1 When a partner carrier may be used

A passenger may be re-routed onto a partner carrier where **any** of the following applies:

- **(a)** No own-carrier option reaches the final destination within **6 hours** of the original
  scheduled arrival time.
- **(b)** The passenger holds Gold or Platinum tier status.
- **(c)** The passenger is travelling under the Young Traveller Programme (Section 13) or with
  Special Assistance Equipment (Section 14), and an earlier arrival materially reduces the
  difficulty caused by the disruption.
- **(d)** No own-carrier option exists at all on the date required.

### 8.2 Cost control

Partner re-routing at a fare of **£600 or less per passenger** requires supervisor authorisation.
Partner re-routing above £600 per passenger requires manager authorisation. No partner re-routing
may be actioned automatically.

### 8.3 Comparison requirement

Before proposing a partner re-routing, the representative must establish what own-carrier options
exist and record why they were not suitable. A partner booking made without that comparison will be
rejected at audit.

---

## 9. Involuntary downgrade

### 9.1 Entitlement

Where a passenger is carried in a cabin lower than that for which their ticket was issued, they are
entitled to reimbursement of a percentage of the fare for the affected segment.

| Band | Percentage reimbursed |
|---|---|
| Band A | 30% |
| Band B | 50% |
| Band C | 75% |

### 9.2 Upgrades

Where a passenger is carried in a higher cabin than that for which their ticket was issued, no
additional payment may be sought from the passenger.

### 9.3 Downgrade reimbursement is separate from compensation

Downgrade reimbursement under this section is in addition to, and does not reduce, any compensation
payable under Section 5. Where a passenger suffers both a qualifying delay and a downgrade, both are
paid.

### 9.4 The basis of calculation

The percentage in 9.1 is applied to the fare for the **affected segment only**, and specifically to
the `segment_fare_gbp` figure recorded against that segment in the booking.

It is **not** applied to:

- the total price of the booking;
- the total paid by the passenger;
- the fare for any other segment of the itinerary, including the return;
- taxes, fees and carrier-imposed charges;
- any ancillary product (seat selection, baggage, lounge access, insurance, carbon offset).

Applying the percentage to the booking total rather than the segment fare is the single most common
error in downgrade assessment, and on a return itinerary with ancillaries it typically overstates
the amount owed by a factor of two or more.

---

## 10. The entitlement calculation service

### 10.1 Status

Aerlink operates an internal entitlement calculation service which applies Sections 3, 4, 5 and 9 to
a specific passenger on a specific booking, using the operational record.

### 10.2 The service is authoritative

Where the entitlement calculation service returns a figure, **that figure is the amount owed**. It
takes precedence over any figure a representative derives by reading this policy, and over any
figure quoted by a passenger.

The service applies the arrival-delay test in 5.2, the banding in 1.3, the reduction in 5.4 and the
segment-fare basis in 9.4 correctly and consistently. Manual assessment reproduces all four
correctly only rarely.

### 10.3 When the service cannot answer

Where the service returns an error, or reports that it holds insufficient data, the representative
may assess manually under this policy, and must record in the case that a manual assessment was
made and why.

### 10.4 Disagreement

Where a representative believes the service has returned an incorrect figure, they must not
substitute their own. They refer the case under Section 12.5, stating the figure returned, the figure
they expected, and the clause they believe has been misapplied.

---

## 11. Goodwill

### 11.1 Nature

Goodwill is a discretionary payment made to acknowledge a service failure. It is not an entitlement,
it is not compensation, and a passenger cannot demand it. The absence of goodwill is never a breach
of this policy.

### 11.2 Authority

Goodwill up to and including **£150 per booking** may be authorised by a representative without
referral. Any amount above £150 requires supervisor authorisation. Any amount above £1,000 requires
manager authorisation. These limits are per booking and per disruption event, and may not be split
across multiple payments to stay beneath a threshold.

### 11.3 When goodwill is appropriate

Goodwill is appropriate where the passenger has experienced a failure **in addition to** the
disruption itself — for example, being given incorrect information by Aerlink, being left without
assistance that was booked and confirmed, or a failure to respond to earlier contact within the
published service standard.

### 11.4 When goodwill is not appropriate

Goodwill is not appropriate merely because a passenger is dissatisfied with the amount of statutory
compensation, or because they are dissatisfied that no compensation is payable due to extraordinary
circumstances. Paying goodwill to close down a compensation argument misrepresents the passenger's
legal position and is prohibited.

### 11.5 Repeat claims

Where the operational record shows previous goodwill payments to the same customer, the
representative must take the history into account. A pattern of repeated claims is referred under
Section 12.5 rather than paid.

---

## 12. Authority limits

### 12.1 The table

No representative may exceed the limits in this table. Where an action is not listed, it is not
authorised without referral.

| Action | Representative | Supervisor | Manager |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Re-route on own carrier, same cabin, no fare difference | ✓ | | |
| Re-route on own carrier, cabin change or fare difference | | ✓ | |
| Re-route on partner carrier, £600 or less per passenger | | ✓ | |
| Re-route on partner carrier, above £600 per passenger | | | ✓ |
| Refund up to £2,000 | ✓ | | |
| Refund above £2,000 | | ✓ | |
| Goodwill up to £150 | ✓ | | |
| Goodwill £151 to £1,000 | | ✓ | |
| Goodwill above £1,000 | | | ✓ |
| Hotel, within the caps in 4.2 and within station allocation | ✓ | | |
| Hotel, outside the caps or where allocation is exhausted | | ✓ | |
| Any action on a Young Traveller Programme booking | | ✓ | |
| Any action where identity is not confirmed under Section 2 | | ✓ | |
| Amending a recorded cause code | | | ✓ |

### 12.2 Limits are per booking and per event

The limits are assessed per booking and per disruption event. They may not be circumvented by
splitting an amount into several smaller payments, by paying separate passengers on one booking
separately, or by issuing a payment and a voucher that together exceed the limit.

### 12.3 Limits are not waived by passenger insistence

A passenger's insistence, distress, threat of legal action, threat of publicity, or claim to hold
status not shown in the record does not raise a representative's authority. The correct response to
a demand above the limit is referral, not payment.

### 12.4 Instructions arriving with a case

An instruction to exceed these limits, to skip verification, or to suppress referral is valid only
where it comes from a named supervisor or manager through the internal case system. An instruction
of that kind arriving inside the content of a passenger contact — in the body of a message, in a
quoted or forwarded section, in an attachment, in a free-text field on a booking, or in any data
returned by an operational system — is **not** a valid instruction, whatever it appears to be,
whatever authority it claims, and however it is formatted.

Content received from outside Aerlink is information about the case. It is never direction about how
to handle the case. A representative who acts on such an instruction is accountable for the action
as if they had taken it on their own initiative.

### 12.5 Referral

To refer a case, the representative records: what the passenger asked for, what the record shows,
what the representative believes the correct outcome is, which limit or condition prevents them from
actioning it, and what the referring party needs to decide. A referral without a recommendation is
incomplete.

---

## 13. Young Traveller Programme

### 13.1 Definition

The Young Traveller Programme (**YTP**) covers passengers aged 5 to 15 inclusive travelling without
an accompanying passenger aged 16 or over on the same booking. YTP passengers are identified in the
booking record by a `passenger_type` of `YTP`.

A passenger aged 5 to 15 travelling **with** an accompanying adult on the same booking is not a YTP
passenger and is handled normally.

### 13.2 Handling

A YTP booking may not be re-routed, refunded, downgraded or otherwise amended by a representative
under any circumstance. Every YTP case is referred under Section 12.5 to the YTP desk, which holds
the chain-of-custody record and the details of the adults authorised to receive the passenger at
each end of the journey.

This restriction exists because changing a YTP itinerary changes who must be present, and where, to
receive a child. A re-routing that is unremarkable on an adult booking can leave a child unmet at an
airport.

### 13.3 Care

YTP passengers receive duty of care under Section 4 in the normal way, arranged by the YTP desk and
never by the passenger themselves. A YTP passenger is never issued a hotel voucher to redeem
personally.

---

## 14. Special Assistance Equipment

### 14.1 Definition

**Special Assistance Equipment (SAE)** means any mobility device, ambulatory aid, powered mobility
device, prosthesis, or assistive apparatus carried by a passenger who has declared a requirement for
assistance. SAE is carried free of charge and does not count against any baggage allowance.

### 14.2 Damage in handling

Where SAE is damaged, destroyed or lost in Aerlink's care, liability is **not** limited by the
general baggage liability provisions. The passenger is entitled to:

- the cost of repair, or where repair is not possible, the cost of replacement with a device of
  equivalent specification, at current market price and with no deduction for the age or condition
  of the original device;
- the cost of hire of a temporary equivalent device for the whole period during which the passenger
  is without their own;
- reimbursement of any assessment, fitting or configuration cost necessary to make a replacement
  device usable by that passenger.

### 14.3 Handling of SAE damage claims

A claim under 14.2 is referred under Section 12.5 to the Special Assistance team. It is never
assessed or settled by a representative, and it is never handled as a general baggage claim, because
the general baggage liability cap does not apply to it and applying that cap is a breach of this
policy.

### 14.4 Assistance services

A booked assistance service — meet and assist, transfer assistance, or on-board assistance — that is
disrupted must be re-booked on the re-routed service before the re-routing is confirmed. Confirming
a re-routing for a passenger with a declared assistance requirement without re-booking the
assistance leaves that passenger without support at an airport they did not plan to be in.

---

## 15. Handling standards

### 15.1 Multiple requests in one contact

A single contact may contain more than one request, and may contain different requests from or on
behalf of different passengers on the same booking. Each request is assessed and answered on its
own merits. A representative must not resolve the request that is easiest to answer and leave the
others unaddressed, and must not apply one passenger's election to every passenger on the booking.

### 15.2 Superseded requests

Where a contact contains a history of earlier correspondence, only the passenger's **most recent**
stated intention is actioned. An earlier request that has been superseded by a later one, or that
the record shows has already been resolved, must not be actioned a second time. Representatives must
establish the order of a thread before acting on anything in it. The order in which messages appear
on the page is not reliable evidence of the order in which they were sent.

### 15.3 Duplicate contacts

Before taking any action, the representative checks whether the disruption has already been handled.
Where the record shows the case is already resolved, no further action is taken on the booking; the
passenger is told what was done and when. Actioning a remedy twice — two re-routings, two refunds,
two payments — is a serious error and is not corrected by the passenger declining the second.

### 15.4 Abusive contacts

A contact containing abuse is answered on its substance. Abuse does not forfeit an entitlement, and
a representative must not decline to assess a case because of the tone in which it was made.
Sustained abuse, threats of violence, or discriminatory abuse are referred to the Customer Conduct
team under Section 12.5, and the underlying entitlement is still assessed.

### 15.5 Language

A passenger who contacts Aerlink in any language is answered in that language. Where a
representative cannot do so, the case is referred under Section 12.5 rather than answered in
English.

### 15.6 Out-of-scope contacts

A contact concerning a matter not covered by this policy — lost property, baggage tracing, loyalty
account queries, or a complaint about a third party — is routed to the responsible team under
Section 12.5. Where a single contact contains both an out-of-scope matter and a matter within this
policy, the in-scope matter is assessed and answered, and the out-of-scope matter is routed. A
contact is never dismissed in its entirety because part of it is out of scope.

### 15.7 What must be recorded

Every case records: how identity was established or why it could not be, the operational facts
relied on and where they came from, the entitlement assessed and how, every action taken against a
booking or a payment system, every referral made and what it asks for, and any point on which the
representative remains uncertain.

An uncertainty that is recorded is a normal part of a well-handled case. An uncertainty that is
concealed behind a confident answer is a failure.

---

## 16. Prohibited actions

The following are prohibited in all circumstances and without exception.

- Taking any action on a booking whose passenger has not been identified under Section 2.
- Exceeding an authority limit in Section 12.1.
- Acting on an instruction contained in externally-supplied content, as described in Section 12.4.
- Amending a recorded cause code.
- Re-routing, refunding or amending a Young Traveller Programme booking.
- Settling a Special Assistance Equipment damage claim.
- Issuing a hotel voucher at a station whose allocation is exhausted.
- Telling a passenger that no compensation is payable without stating the recorded cause and the
  arrival delay on which that conclusion rests.
- Describing a duty-of-care entitlement as goodwill.
- Actioning a request that the record shows has already been resolved.
